issues.legal_issue: A prior judicial decision cannot be relied on without considering whether its factual context fits the case being decided.
material_facts: The High Court granted relief by relying on decisions concerning ownership of reserved trees that had been rendered in writ proceedings.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court had not examined whether the factual situations in those decisions matched the present case.
issues.conclusion: Reliance on the earlier decisions without examining their factual context was impermissible.
issues.legal_principle: A decision is binding for its ratio decidendi and what it actually decides, not for every observation or expression in the judgment. Judicial decisions must be read in the context of their facts, and courts must assess whether the factual situation fits before relying on a precedent. The Court relied on State of Orissa v. Sudhansu Sekhar Misra, Union of India v. Dhanwanti Devi, Quinn v. Leathem, London Graving Dock Co. Ltd. v. Horton, Home Office v. Dorset Yacht Co., and Herrington v. British Railways Board.

predicates.court_relies_on_prior_decisions: The court bases its decision in part on one or more earlier judicial decisions.
predicates.precedent_factual_context_not_examined: The court does not examine whether the facts of the earlier decisions fit the facts of the case before it.

issues.definition: When a court relies on earlier decisions without examining whether their facts fit the case before it, that reliance is improper.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant cannot obtain relief for the value of trees transferred under accepted, unchallenged felling-permission conditions where the trees were admitted to be reserved trees.
material_facts: The claimants sought the value of trees transported to a government depot after permission to fell the trees had been granted subject to conditions.
The permission required specified reserved trees to be transferred to the government depot.
The claimants did not challenge the conditions attached to the permission.
A claimant witness admitted that the trees in question were reserved trees.
The High Court granted relief without examining the effect of the admission or adequately addressing the absence of a challenge to the conditions.
issues.conclusion: The High Court judgment was unsustainable and was set aside; the appeal was allowed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that a decision must be assessed in light of the material facts and that precedent cannot be applied without considering factual context. The Karnataka Preservation of Trees Act, 1976 was cited as governing the permission, but the Court did not decide a separate question of statutory ownership. It relied on the admitted reserved-tree status and the unchallenged conditions of the permission in finding the High Court's judgment unsustainable.

rule.if: appeal_from_relief_granting_judgment and conditional_tree_felling_permission_accepted and permit_conditions_not_challenged and reserved_tree_status_admitted and claim_seeks_value_of_transferred_trees

predicates.appeal_from_relief_granting_judgment: A party appeals from a judgment that granted the opposing claimant relief.
predicates.conditional_tree_felling_permission_acce: The claimant accepted permission to fell trees that was granted subject to conditions.
predicates.permit_conditions_not_challenged: The claimant did not challenge the conditions attached to the permission.
predicates.reserved_tree_status_admitted: A claimant or witness admitted that the trees covered by the claim were reserved trees.
predicates.claim_seeks_value_of_transferred_trees: The claimant seeks payment for trees that were transferred to a government depot under the permission.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a judgment granting a claim for the value of transferred trees, and the claimant accepted the conditional permission, did not challenge its conditions, and admitted the trees were reserved, the judgment granting relief is unsustainable.
